script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the newly restored Corran Hall. My name's Fiona, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. The tour will take about an hour.

You're welcome to take photographs almost everywhere, including the main auditorium and the backstage area. The one exception is the archive room, because some of the old papers there can be damaged by camera flash.

Let's start with a little history. The hall opened in eighteen ninety-one. It's named after the composer Edmund Corran, but he never actually gave any money towards it. In fact, the building was paid for by a group of local wool merchants.
Many people assume the town council built it, but the council only bought the hall in the nineteen-fifties, when the merchants' families could no longer afford to run it.

So why did it close? There was a small fire on the stage in the nineteen-sixties, and by the nineteen-nineties the roof was leaking quite badly. But neither of those things shut the doors. The hall finally closed in two thousand and nine, when inspectors discovered that the balcony was no longer safe.

The restoration took six years and cost thirty-eight million pounds. You might think raising that money was the hardest part, but the project director says the real difficulty was finding people with the skills to repair the decorated plaster ceiling.
In the end, the team had to train a group of apprentices from scratch, and several of them now work on other historic buildings around the country.
Now, if you look at the seats, you'll notice they're new. People often ask whether they were chosen for comfort, or to match the deep red of the originals.

Actually, they were designed so that each empty seat absorbs about the same amount of sound as a person sitting in it. That means an orchestra rehearsing in an empty hall hears almost exactly what the audience will hear on the night.
Above the stage you can see the organ, which has over four thousand pipes. It's being tuned at the moment, so I'm afraid we can't play it at the end of the tour as we used to.
And it isn't used during the evening concerts this season either. But if you'd like to hear it, there's a free recital every Friday at lunchtime.
Finally, a few practical points. The café in the foyer is open until five. Your tour ticket doesn't include a drink there, I'm afraid, but it does give you ten per cent off anything in the gift shop.
Right, if everyone's ready, let's walk through to the auditorium.
listening.title: Part 2 · A tour of a restored concert hall

paragraphs: A. For most of the twentieth century, urban noise was treated as an unavoidable by-product of economic growth. Traffic, construction and industry were expected to be loud, and city dwellers were expected to put up with them. Complaints were handled one at a time, usually by measuring the volume of a particular source and deciding whether it exceeded a legal limit. This approach, many researchers now argue, missed something important: it described noise only as a quantity to be reduced, rather than as one part of a wider sound environment that people experience as a whole.

B. The concept of the 'soundscape' emerged to fill this gap. Instead of asking simply how loud a place is, soundscape researchers ask what can be heard there and how people feel about it. A square with a fountain and children playing may register a higher decibel level than a quiet road beside a motorway, yet most people describe the first as far more pleasant. In a 2019 survey of 2,400 residents in the northern port city of Velmore, participants listened to recordings made in their own neighbourhoods and rated how satisfied they felt. The character of the sounds predicted their satisfaction far more accurately than the measured volume did.

C. The health effects of unwanted noise are now well documented. Long-term exposure to night-time traffic has been linked to disturbed sleep, raised blood pressure and an increased risk of heart disease. According to Dr Ines Halvorsen, an acoustician at Velmore University, the body reacts to sudden sounds even during sleep, without the sleeper waking up. 'People tell us they have got used to the traffic,' she says, 'but their heart rate tells a different story.' Her team found that residents who had lived beside busy roads for more than ten years showed the same physical responses at night as people who had only recently moved in.

D. In response, a number of European cities have begun to protect what they call 'quiet zones': parks, courtyards and riverbanks where noise is kept low by restricting traffic and banning amplified music. Velmore created its first eleven zones in 2015. Unusually, the locations were not chosen by engineers alone. Residents were invited to nominate places they already visited to escape the noise, and around half of the final list came from these suggestions. The council reports that visitor numbers rose by roughly a third in the first two years, although it admits that visitors were not counted in the same way before the scheme began, so the figure should be treated with some caution.

E. Interestingly, complete silence is not the goal. Spaces with no sound at all can feel uncomfortable, even threatening, and studies suggest that people are most at ease where natural sounds such as birdsong, running water or wind in the trees can be heard. Designers have therefore developed a technique known as masking, in which pleasant sounds are added to cover unwanted ones. A water feature in a busy square, for example, can make nearby traffic much less noticeable. However, masking only works if the added sound is no louder than the noise it is meant to hide; a badly designed fountain can simply add to the din.

F. Quiet also appears to have a measurable economic value. A study of property sales in Velmore found that flats overlooking a quiet inner courtyard sold for around eight per cent more than similar flats facing the street. Some economists now argue that the cost of noise should be included whenever new roads or railways are evaluated. Critics, however, warn that turning quiet into a valuable commodity could push up housing costs in calm districts and force lower-income households into noisier ones, a pattern some have called 'acoustic inequality'.

G. For Halvorsen, the main lesson is that planners must consider sound at the design stage, not after a building or street has been completed. The shape of buildings, the materials used and even the position of bedrooms on the quieter side of a block can make a significant difference. 'Nobody would design a house and only then decide where the windows should go,' she says. 'Sound deserves the same early attention.' Relatively simple measures, from low-noise road surfaces to electric buses, could allow cities to sound as good as they look.

script: Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for coming. I'm Priya, the volunteer coordinator here at the Eastgate Food Bank, and this short talk will tell you what to expect over the next few weeks.

First, a little background. The food bank was started eleven years ago by a group of parents from a local church hall. Many people assume the council set it up, but in fact we've never received regular council funding; most of our money comes from individual donors and two local supermarkets.

Now, the building. When you arrive for a shift, please come in through the side door on Carver Street, not the main entrance. The main entrance is reserved for the people who come to collect food parcels, and we want them to feel it's their space.

The first thing you do on arrival is sign in on the tablet by the kitchen. We used to have a paper book, and some of you may remember it, but the tablet lets us know exactly who is in the building if there's a fire alarm.

Most of you will start in the sorting room. Donated food arrives in mixed bags, and your job is to check each item. Dented tins are fine, and so is food a few days past its 'best before' date. But anything past its 'use by' date must go straight in the red bin, without exception.

Some of you have asked about working with clients directly. That's something we'd love you to do eventually, but only after you've completed at least six sorting shifts and a short listening course, which runs on Wednesday evenings.

A quick word about clothing. You don't need anything special, but closed shoes are essential, because we move heavy crates around and things do get dropped. Aprons are provided, so there's no need to bring your own, and we ask you not to wear perfume, as some clients have allergies.

Our busiest time of year, perhaps surprisingly, isn't Christmas, when donations are high. It's actually the summer holidays, when children don't get free school meals and families need far more support. So if you can give extra hours in July and August, that's when it really matters.

Finally, parking. There's no parking on site, I'm afraid. The supermarket car park nearby is free for two hours, but shifts are three hours long, so we'd really encourage you to come by bus. The number fourteen stops right outside.

If you're unable to come to a shift, please text the coordinator's phone rather than emailing, because emails often aren't read until the evening. Right, let's take a short break, and then I'll show you round the sorting room.
Oh, and help yourselves to tea and coffee. The biscuits, I should say, are not from the donations; they were bought specially for today.
And don't worry about remembering everything. You'll each be paired with an experienced volunteer for your first three shifts.

paragraphs: A. Long before anyone understood what a microbe was, people across the world were relying on invisible organisms to make their food safer, tastier and longer-lasting. Fermentation is the process by which bacteria and yeasts break down sugars in the absence of oxygen, producing acids, gases or alcohol as by-products. These by-products are what give sourdough its tang, yoghurt its thickness and kimchi its sharp, sour bite. Crucially, many of them also create conditions in which harmful organisms struggle to survive.

B. The oldest firm evidence of deliberate fermentation comes from residues found inside clay jars, which suggest that people were brewing drinks from rice, honey and fruit some nine thousand years ago. Bread arrived somewhat later. According to the food historian Ilse Marchetti, early bakers probably discovered leavening by accident, when a batch of dough was left standing and wild yeasts from the air settled on it. The dough rose, the bread was lighter, and the baker kept back a small piece to start the next batch. This practice of saving a 'starter' continues today, and some bakeries claim their starters have been fed continuously for more than a century.

C. The chemistry of preservation is surprisingly simple. In yoghurt, for example, lactic acid bacteria convert milk sugar into lactic acid. As the acid builds up, the milk becomes too sour for most spoilage bacteria, and the milk proteins tighten into a soft gel. Vegetables are preserved in a similar way. When cabbage is packed tightly with salt, the salt draws water out of the leaves and suppresses unwanted microbes, while salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria multiply. Within a few days the brine becomes acidic enough to protect the vegetables for months.

D. Before refrigeration, these techniques were essential to survival in many regions. In Korea, households traditionally made large quantities of kimchi in late autumn in a communal event known as gimjang, when families and neighbours gathered to salt and season hundreds of cabbages. The finished kimchi was stored in earthenware pots, which were often partly buried in the ground. Here the soil kept the temperature low and stable, slowing fermentation so that the vegetables remained edible throughout the winter. Similar methods developed independently in central Europe, where sauerkraut sustained communities through months without fresh produce.

E. The arrival of domestic refrigerators in the twentieth century changed eating habits dramatically. Because food could now be kept cold, the need to ferment it largely disappeared in wealthier countries, and many home traditions faded within a generation. A survey carried out by the Northfield Food Institute in 1998 found that fewer than one in twenty households in the region it studied still made any fermented food at home, compared with almost half in the 1950s. Factory-made versions, meanwhile, were often pasteurised after production, a heating process that kills the living bacteria.

F. In recent years, however, interest has returned. Part of the reason is flavour: chefs value the complex, savoury notes that slow fermentation creates. Another factor is health. Some studies suggest that live bacteria in fermented foods may support the community of microbes in the human gut, although researchers caution that the evidence remains limited. Dr Tomas Oyelaran, a microbiologist, argues that many popular claims are 'running well ahead of the science', and that the benefits probably vary greatly between individuals and between products.

G. Home fermentation is not without risk. If too little salt is used, or if vegetables are exposed to air, moulds and harmful bacteria can grow before the brine becomes acidic. For this reason, food safety advisers recommend measuring salt by weight rather than by the spoonful, keeping vegetables fully submerged, and discarding any batch that smells rotten rather than pleasantly sour. Followed carefully, though, these simple rules allow modern cooks to practise one of humanity's oldest kitchen technologies.

script: Morning, everyone, and welcome to Brackenfell National Park. My name's Isla, and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you set off on the Corrie Ridge trail, I'd like to spend ten minutes going through some safety points. The full circuit is about eleven kilometres, and most groups take around five hours.

First, the weather. The forecast is dry all day, and the wind on the summit is expected to be fairly light, which is good news. The thing that concerns me is that low cloud is likely to come down after about two o'clock this afternoon. When that happens the ridge can disappear in minutes, and it becomes very hard to see the path.
Now, equipment. Please carry at least two litres of water each and a spare warm layer. Waterproof trousers are a good idea, and I'll be handing out a free map to every group in a moment.

Some of you have walking poles, which are certainly helpful on the descent, but they're not essential. The one thing I won't let anyone start without, though, is a pair of proper boots with ankle support. Trainers just aren't safe on the loose stones near the top.

As for finding your way, the route is marked with wooden posts with yellow tops. You'll also notice white paint marks on some of the rocks. Please ignore those. They show an old path that we closed because of erosion.

For the first part of the walk you'll be following a stream, and later there's a long stone wall on your left, but neither of those stays with the trail all the way, so keep looking for the yellow posts.

About two thirds of the way up you'll reach a stone shelter at a place called Haws Gap. This is important. If you get there later than one o'clock, I want you to turn back the way you came, even if the summit looks close.
You may notice a lower path from the shelter on the map, but it's flooded at the moment, so please don't take it as a shortcut. And there's no need to phone us to ask permission. Just turn round.
Talking of phones, the signal up there is poor. Surprisingly, there's almost nothing in the car park, and in the forest it comes and goes. The only place you can really rely on is the summit itself.
If there's an emergency, dial nine nine nine, ask for the police, and then ask for mountain rescue.

A word for dog owners. You'll need to keep dogs on a lead between March and July. There haven't been any sheep on the ridge for several years now, so that's not the reason. It's because rare birds nest on the ground up there at this time of year, and a dog can easily disturb them.

Finally, there's a board outside the visitor centre. Please write your group's name on it before you leave and sign it again when you get back. It isn't for counting visitors. We have an electronic sensor on the gate for that.

The point is that if a name hasn't been signed off by seven o'clock this evening, we'll assume that group is in difficulty and begin a search. So please don't forget, or you could end up with a rescue team looking for you while you're having dinner in the village.
Right, that's everything from me. Collect your maps from the desk, and enjoy the walk.

paragraphs: A. Ask someone how they get from home to work and the answer usually takes one of two forms. Some people describe a chain of actions: turn left at the bakery, continue past the petrol station, take the second right. Others describe the layout of the area as if looking down on it from above: the office lies north of the river, roughly halfway between the park and the hospital. Psychologists call the first approach route-based navigation and the second survey-based navigation. The idea that the brain stores something like an internal plan of the environment, known as a cognitive map, was first proposed in the middle of the twentieth century by researchers who noticed that rats in mazes could take shortcuts they had never been trained to use.

B. Since then, neuroscientists have located much of the machinery behind these maps in the hippocampus, a curved structure deep inside the brain. In a study at the University of Halden, researchers scanned the brains of sixty bicycle couriers who had spent years memorising the streets of a large, irregular city. Compared with office workers of the same age, the couriers had more grey matter in the rear part of the hippocampus, and the difference was greatest among those who had worked in the job the longest. The couriers also scored higher on tests of spatial memory, although they were no better than average at remembering lists of words or faces.

C. Not everyone navigates in the same way. Some people rely heavily on landmarks, while others keep track of direction and distance as they move, a process known as path integration. When volunteers are asked to rate their own sense of direction, their answers turn out to be surprisingly accurate predictors of how they perform on real navigation tasks. Culture and language also play a part. In several communities whose languages describe positions using compass points rather than words such as 'left' and 'right', even young children can point towards distant places with remarkable precision.

D. These findings raise a question that matters to almost anyone with a smartphone: does relying on satellite navigation weaken our natural abilities? In one experiment at the Brennholt Institute of Spatial Cognition, forty-eight volunteers drove through an unfamiliar virtual town in a driving simulator. Half followed spoken turn-by-turn instructions; the other half studied a paper map beforehand. The guided drivers made no more wrong turns than the others and actually reached their destination slightly sooner. Afterwards, however, they recalled far fewer of the landmarks they had passed, and the sketch maps they drew of the town were much less accurate. Interestingly, both groups reported feeling equally relaxed during the drive.

E. Laboratory studies capture only a single journey, so a team led by Dr Ana Vasquez-Lund followed 140 regular drivers over three years. Those who used satellite navigation most heavily showed a steeper decline in spatial memory over the period, and the decline could not be explained by age. Yet Vasquez-Lund is cautious about the conclusion. People who already find navigation difficult may simply be more likely to depend on their devices, she points out, so weak spatial memory might be a cause of heavy use rather than a consequence of it. Although the sample was reasonably large and the study lasted longer than most, only a carefully controlled experiment could settle the matter.

F. None of this means that satellite navigation is simply harmful. Surveys suggest that it gives many people, particularly older drivers and new arrivals in a city, the confidence to explore neighbourhoods they would otherwise avoid. Some designers now argue that the problem lies not in the technology itself but in the way instructions are delivered. Experimental systems that mention landmarks ('turn right after the red church') rather than distances ('turn right in 200 metres') appear to help users build a mental picture of their surroundings while still guiding them reliably.

G. For individuals, the practical advice from researchers is modest. Few suggest abandoning digital maps altogether. Instead, they recommend switching the device off on familiar journeys, studying the route before setting out, and occasionally trying to find the way without help. Like many other mental skills, the ability to navigate seems to respond to practice, and the cost of a few wrong turns may be a small price to pay for keeping it.

script: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the visitor centre at Harrowdale Observatory. My name's Imogen, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before we go up to the telescope dome, I'd like to tell you a little about the observatory and how tonight's visit will work.

The observatory was opened in nineteen fifty-eight. Many visitors assume it was built by the university, but in fact it was paid for by a local astronomy society, whose members raised the money through concerts and raffles. The university only took over the running of the site in the nineteen nineties.

Harrowdale was chosen because it sits on high ground, well above the valley fog. People sometimes think it was chosen for being far from any town, but Kelsby is only twelve kilometres away. It was the height that mattered.

The main telescope you'll see tonight is not the original one. The first telescope was moved to a science museum in two thousand and four, and the current instrument, which is about twice the size, was installed the following year.
Now, a few practical points. We'll spend around forty minutes in the dome. It isn't heated, so I'd strongly recommend keeping your coats on, even though it feels warm in here.

Inside the dome, please don't use the flash on your phones. It's not that it damages the telescope, as some people think, but it takes your eyes up to twenty minutes to adjust to the darkness again, so one flash spoils the view for everyone.

If the sky is clear, we'll begin with the Moon, and then, depending on the time, we'll try to find Saturn. We'd hoped to show you a comet that's been in the news, but unfortunately it's too close to the horizon this month.

If clouds do roll in, and that happens quite often here, we'll move to the planetarium room, where my colleague Marcus will give a short show about the life of stars. Your ticket includes that show either way.

The visitor centre itself has had some changes this year. The café is now open on viewing evenings, and the shop has a new range of star maps designed by children from the local primary school. All the profits from those go to the school's science club.

Finally, a lot of you have asked about our monthly membership. Members can book places on evening sessions before the general public, which is useful because they sell out quickly. They don't get free entry, I'm afraid, but they do receive a quarterly newsletter.

Membership also gives you access to our Saturday workshops, where you can learn to use a small telescope yourself. Those workshops are held in the morning, actually, when we look at the Sun through special filters, rather than at night.

And one last thing: there are toilets on the ground floor, next to the café, but there are none in the dome itself, so this would be a good moment to use them. Right, if everyone's ready, please follow me up the stairs.

paragraphs: A. For most of human history, the night sky was a shared inheritance. Anyone stepping outside on a clear evening could see thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way. Today, however, researchers estimate that more than half of the world's population lives under skies so brightened by artificial light that the Milky Way is no longer visible to them. This phenomenon, known as light pollution, has grown steadily since the spread of electric street lighting, and satellite surveys suggest that the area of artificially lit land is still increasing by around two per cent each year.

B. The consequences for wildlife can be severe. Many animals rely on natural cycles of light and darkness to regulate feeding, migration and reproduction. Newly hatched sea turtles, for example, find their way to the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, which on an undeveloped beach is the sky above the water. Where hotels and roads line the shore, hatchlings may crawl inland instead and die of exhaustion. Migrating birds, which often navigate partly by the stars, can become disoriented by brightly lit buildings, and millions are thought to die each year in collisions with towers and office blocks.

C. Insects are perhaps the most affected group of all. A single street lamp can attract moths from a wide area, where they circle until they are exhausted or eaten. Because many night-flying insects pollinate plants, ecologists have begun to ask whether artificial light might be reducing the reproduction of some wild flowers. One field experiment in a rural valley found that meadows lit by temporary lamps received far fewer visits from night-time pollinators than dark meadows nearby, although the long-term effect on plant populations remains uncertain.

D. Human beings are not immune. Exposure to light in the evening, particularly the blue-rich light emitted by many modern LED lamps and screens, suppresses the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps to prepare the body for sleep. Several studies have linked brightly lit bedrooms and streets to shorter and poorer-quality sleep. Medical researchers are cautious, however: while some have proposed connections between night-time light and conditions such as obesity, they point out that people living in brightly lit areas also tend to differ in diet, income and working hours, making it difficult to identify light as the sole cause.

E. For astronomers, the problem is both practical and cultural. Professional observatories have increasingly been built on remote mountains, far from cities, simply to escape the glow. Amateur astronomers have fewer options, and many report that objects they could observe from their gardens as children have now vanished. Some writers argue that something less measurable has also been lost: the experience of a truly dark sky, which inspired early navigation, calendars and countless myths.

F. In response, a growing number of places have been recognised as dark-sky reserves. To qualify, an area must have an exceptionally dark core, usually a national park or protected landscape, surrounded by communities that agree to control their lighting. In practice, this means fitting lamps that point downwards rather than spreading light sideways, choosing warmer colours, and switching off or dimming lights late at night. Several reserves report that such measures have also reduced energy bills, and some rural areas have discovered that 'astro-tourism' brings visitors outside the traditional summer season.

G. Nevertheless, solutions are not always welcomed. Residents sometimes fear that dimmer streets will lead to more crime or road accidents, even though evidence from towns that have reduced their lighting has so far been mixed rather than alarming. Supporters of dark skies therefore stress that the aim is not to plunge communities into darkness but to use light more carefully. As one campaigner put it, the goal is simply to put light where it is needed, when it is needed, and nowhere else.

script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to this session on managing your money. My name is Dr Helen Rourke, and I'm one of the student advisers here at Ashcombe University. Over the next twenty minutes or so, I'd like to give you some practical advice on budgeting during your first year.

Let me start with something that surprises many new students. When we surveyed last year's first-years, the biggest single cause of money problems wasn't rent, and it wasn't tuition-related costs like books. It was food, and in particular buying lunch and snacks on campus every day.

So the first thing I'd recommend is to work out a weekly budget rather than a monthly one. Most of you will receive your loan or your allowance once a term, and a month is simply too long a period to keep track of. A week is much easier to manage.

Some of you may already use a budgeting app, and that's fine. But in our experience, students who simply write down every purchase in a notebook for the first four weeks learn far more about their own habits. The act of writing it down makes you notice what you're spending.

Now, a word about bank accounts. Many banks offer student accounts with gifts, such as a free railcard or vouchers. These can be attractive, but the most important thing to compare is actually the size of the interest-free overdraft, because that's what will protect you if you run short.
However, please don't think of an overdraft as extra income. It's a loan, and it has to be paid back once you graduate.

Next, part-time work. A job can certainly help, and the university's own job shop advertises positions on campus. But we strongly advise first-years not to work more than fifteen hours a week during term, because beyond that point, students' marks tend to fall.

Let's talk about textbooks briefly. Before you buy anything, check the reading list with your tutor. Many of the books are available in the library, and the Students' Union runs a second-hand book sale in the second week of term, where prices are often a third of the original cost.

And one more saving that people often miss: the city's bus company offers a discounted annual pass for students. It costs one hundred and ninety pounds, which sounds like a lot, but if you take the bus every day it works out much cheaper than buying single tickets.

paragraphs: A. In many wealthy economies, the coins and notes that once filled wallets are quietly disappearing. In the imaginary but representative country of Norvania, cash accounted for almost two-thirds of shop transactions in 2012; a decade later, the figure had fallen to under one in eight. Contactless cards, mobile phone wallets and instant bank transfers have taken its place. For retailers, the advantages are clear: queues move faster and there is less risk of theft. Yet researchers have begun to ask a less obvious question: does the way we pay change how much we spend?

B. The idea that payment methods influence behaviour is not new. As early as the 1990s, consumer psychologists suggested that handing over physical money produces a small but real sense of loss, sometimes described as the 'pain of paying'. When the money is invisible, this discomfort is reduced. A frequently discussed experiment at the fictional Kessler Institute in 2016 asked two groups of volunteers to bid for concert tickets in a mock auction. Those told they must pay by card offered, on average, almost twice as much as those required to pay in cash, even though both groups had been given the same budget.

C. Laboratory findings, however, do not always reflect everyday life, and later field studies have produced a more complicated picture. Dr Ines Marlow, an economist who analysed eighteen months of anonymised bank data from 40,000 households, found that people who switched mainly to contactless cards increased their spending by around six per cent overall. The rise was not evenly spread. Large, planned purchases such as furniture or holidays were almost unaffected, while small, frequent items, especially coffee, snacks and taxi rides, accounted for most of the difference. 'It is the low-value, spontaneous purchase where the friction of cash used to act as a brake,' Marlow concluded.

D. Mobile phone payments appear to strengthen this effect further. Because the phone is always in the user's hand, buying something can take less than two seconds, and many apps store card details so that online purchases require only a single tap. Some designers have deliberately made the process feel rewarding, with cheerful sounds or animations confirming each payment. Critics argue that such features turn spending into a kind of game, although technology companies insist that they simply reduce frustration for customers.

E. Not every consequence of the cashless shift is negative. Digital payments leave a detailed record, and a growing number of banking apps now sort transactions into categories and send alerts when a user approaches a monthly limit. Marlow's data showed that households who regularly used these budgeting tools spent slightly less than they had in their cash-using years. In other words, the same technology that removes the pain of paying can, if used deliberately, restore a degree of awareness. The difficulty is that such tools are optional, and the people who would benefit most from them are often the least likely to switch them on.

F. There are also wider social concerns. Older people, those on low incomes and residents of remote rural areas are more likely to rely on cash, and some have found themselves excluded as shops, car parks and even public toilets stop accepting coins. Consumer groups in Norvania have called for a legal guarantee that essential services must continue to accept cash. Others point out that cash provides a valuable backup when electronic systems fail, as happened during a nationwide network outage that lasted several hours in 2021.

G. Some individuals have responded by deliberately returning to cash for part of their budget. A popular approach, known among its followers as 'envelope budgeting', involves withdrawing a fixed weekly amount for discretionary spending and dividing it into labelled envelopes. When an envelope is empty, spending in that category stops. Supporters claim it restores the visible limits that digital money removed, though no large-scale study has yet tested whether the habit lasts beyond the first few months.

H. What seems clear is that the disappearance of cash is changing more than the way money moves; it is altering the small mental signals that once helped people control their spending. As Marlow puts it, 'We have removed the friction without replacing the feedback.' The challenge for banks, regulators and consumers alike will be to design payment systems that remain convenient while still reminding us, gently, that the money we spend is real.

script: Good morning, and welcome back to Riverbank Radio's community hour. I'm Helen Ashworth from the Dunmere Flood Action Group, and after last winter's floods, I've been asked to talk about some simple ways you can prepare your home before the rainy season really starts.

Let's begin with the most important step, which, surprisingly, costs nothing at all. Many people think the first thing to do is buy sandbags, and they certainly have their place. But our group's advice is to start by signing up for the free flood warning text service. Even two hours' notice gives you time to move valuables upstairs.

Speaking of sandbags, a word of warning. Traditional sandbags are heavy and, once wet, they're often contaminated and have to be thrown away. They also take a long time to fill. That's why more households are choosing flood boards, which fit across doorways. They're more expensive at first, but they can be reused for years.

Now, a question I'm asked a lot: where does water actually get into houses? Most people point to the front door. In fact, according to the surveys our volunteers carried out last spring, the most common entry point in Dunmere was air bricks, those small vents in the outside walls. Covers for these are cheap and easy to fit.

Inside the house, think about what would be hardest to replace. Furniture can usually be claimed on insurance, but family photographs and documents can't. So we recommend keeping them in a sealed plastic box on a high shelf, rather than in a drawer downstairs.

Electricity is another concern. If you're redecorating anyway, it's worth asking an electrician to move sockets higher up the wall, at least a metre above the floor. It isn't something you should attempt yourself, and it's not necessary to rewire the whole house.

Next, the garden. Paving over front gardens for parking has made local flooding worse, because rain can't soak into the ground. If you're planning new paving, choose gravel or permeable blocks instead. And clear leaves from drains and gutters in the autumn, which is when they block most easily.

Of course, preparation isn't only about the building. Put together a small emergency bag with a torch, medicines, phone chargers and copies of your insurance details. Our volunteers recently found that only about one household in five had anything like this ready.

Finally, help is available. The council offers grants for flood protection, but only to homes that flooded in the last five years, and you'll need a survey first. Our group can arrange that survey free of charge, so do get in touch.
We're also holding a drop-in session at the library next Saturday, where you can see flood boards and air brick covers for yourself. I'll be there from ten until two, and there's no need to book.
We'll put all of these tips on the Riverbank Radio website after the programme. Now, I believe we have a few listeners waiting on the phone line, so let's take the first call.
And remember, the best time to prepare is before the water arrives, not after. Thank you.

paragraphs: A. For most of the twentieth century, cities dealt with rainwater as a waste product. Roofs, roads and car parks were designed to shed water as quickly as possible into underground pipes, which carried it to the nearest river. This approach worked reasonably well while cities were small and rainfall was predictable. However, as urban areas have spread and storms have become more intense, many drainage systems have been overwhelmed. When the pipes fill, water backs up into streets and basements, and in older cities rain often mixes with sewage before overflowing into rivers.

B. The idea of the 'sponge city' offers a different philosophy. Instead of removing rain as fast as possible, a sponge city tries to hold it where it falls, allowing it to soak into the ground, evaporate, or be stored for later use. The term became widely known in the 2010s, but the principles are much older. Farmers in many dry regions have long built terraces and ponds to capture seasonal rain, and some historic towns were laid out around ponds and canals that absorbed floodwater. What is new is the attempt to apply these ideas systematically across dense modern cities, where almost every surface has been sealed with concrete or asphalt.

C. In practice, a sponge city combines many small measures rather than relying on a single large structure. Parks can be landscaped with shallow hollows that fill during storms and drain slowly afterwards. Roadside 'rain gardens', planted with grasses and shrubs that tolerate both flooding and drought, collect water running off pavements. Green roofs, covered in a thin layer of soil and plants, can hold a significant share of the rain that falls on them. Perhaps the least visible measure is permeable paving, which allows water to pass through gaps or porous material into a layer of gravel below. From there, the water either seeps slowly into the soil or is carried to storage tanks, where it can later be used to water parks and flush toilets.

D. Supporters argue that these features bring benefits well beyond flood control. Wetland parks provide habitats for birds and insects, and planted areas help to cool streets during heatwaves. In the northern city of Harnvik, for example, planners converted a disused railway yard into a wetland park of eleven hectares. According to the city's own monitoring, the park now stores up to 40,000 cubic metres of water during heavy rain, and surface temperatures nearby are on average two degrees lower in summer than in surrounding districts.

E. Nevertheless, the approach has its critics. Engineers point out that green infrastructure is effective against frequent, moderate storms but can do little during extreme events, when the ground is already saturated. In such cases, conventional pipes, tunnels and flood walls remain essential. Others have raised concerns about cost. Although individual rain gardens are inexpensive, transforming an entire city requires coordination between many departments, and the features must be maintained. A rain garden clogged with silt and litter can stop working within a few years.

F. There are also questions of fairness. Researchers at the Kessling Institute for Urban Studies found that in several cities, new wetland parks raised nearby property prices, sometimes forcing out the lower-income residents the projects were intended to protect. The researchers do not argue against sponge city projects, but recommend that planners involve local communities early and combine green investment with policies that protect affordable housing.

G. Despite these challenges, the sponge city concept is spreading. Rather than requiring dramatic new projects, many authorities now simply change the rules for new developments, requiring builders to manage a fixed proportion of rainfall on their own sites. In the long run, the most important change may be cultural: a shift from seeing rain as a problem to be disposed of to seeing it as a resource to be managed. If that shift takes hold, the streets of future cities may look rather different, with fewer drains and considerably more green space.

script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashcombe Museum of Childhood. My name's Harriet, and I'll be showing you round for the next hour or so. Please keep your tickets with you, as you'll need them to get back in if you pop out to the garden.

Let me start with the building itself. Many visitors assume it must have been a school, because of the tall windows and the bell tower, but in fact it was built in eighteen seventy as a hat factory. The bell was used to call the workers in each morning.

The museum opened here in nineteen sixty-one. It began with a gift from a local doctor, Elsie Brannock, who lived in the house next door. She had spent forty years collecting dolls, around four hundred of them, and she gave the whole collection to the town.

People are sometimes surprised that she didn't give us the tin soldiers you'll see upstairs. Those actually came much later, from a private collector in the nineteen-eighties, along with most of our board games.

Now, a quick word about photography. You're welcome to take pictures almost everywhere, including here in the entrance hall and in the Street of Games. The one exception is the Nursery Gallery. The old baby clothes and quilts in there are extremely fragile, so no photographs at all, with or without flash.

Our first proper stop will be the Street of Games, which is a recreation of a town street from the nineteen-fifties. Children, and adults too, are invited to have a go at the playground games chalked on the pavement, such as hopscotch and marbles.

There's also a little cinema at the end of the street that normally shows a short film about street life, but I'm afraid it's closed for repairs at the moment. And some of you may remember the dressing-up box that used to be there. That was removed last year, sadly, because the costumes had worn out.

After that we'll go past the toy workshop. You might imagine that all our repairs are done by a professional conservator. We do call one in for the most valuable items, but day to day the work is done by a team of retired volunteers, several of whom used to be engineers.
We also have students from the local college who join us in the summer, but they mainly help with cataloguing the collection rather than mending things.

Upstairs, look out for the wooden Noah's Ark with its sixty little animals. It's beautifully finished, and people often think it came from an expensive toy shop. In fact, it was carved by a prisoner of war in nineteen seventeen, as a present for the children of the farmer he was sent to work for.
It isn't our oldest object, by the way. That honour goes to a small spinning top from the seventeen-hundreds, which was found under the floorboards of a cottage in the village.

We'll finish the tour in the Learning Room, where children can make a simple peg doll to take home with them. The café is on the ground floor if you'd like lunch afterwards, though that isn't included in the ticket.
And just so there's no confusion, the shop discount vouchers mentioned on our old leaflets are now for members only. Right, if everyone's ready, follow me through this door on the left.

paragraphs: A. Ask a group of adults to describe their happiest childhood memories and many will mention building dens, exploring waste ground or inventing games with friends far from adult eyes. Psychologists call this kind of activity unstructured play: play in which children decide for themselves what to do, how to do it and when to stop, without goals or rules set by adults. For most of human history it was simply what childhood looked like. Over the past few decades, however, it has become noticeably rarer, and researchers are increasingly asking what children may be losing as a result.

B. One of the most detailed attempts to answer that question was led by the developmental psychologist Dr Miriam Okafor-Lindqvist at the University of Tellbridge. Her team followed 340 children from the age of four to ten, asking families to keep diaries of how their children spent their free time. Children who had more hours of self-directed play tended to score higher on tests of executive function, the set of mental skills that allows people to plan, to switch between tasks and to control their impulses. Okafor-Lindqvist is careful, however, not to overstate her findings. 'We have shown a link, not proof that one causes the other,' she says. 'It may be that children who already have these skills are simply better at organising their own play.'

C. Some of the strongest arguments for free play concern risk. Climbing trees, balancing on walls and play-fighting all carry a small chance of injury, yet researchers believe such activities allow children to test and judge their own limits. A child who climbs a little higher each week, they argue, learns to read both the situation and his or her own feelings of fear. In one trial in New Zealand, several primary schools removed some of their playground rules and allowed pupils to climb trees and ride scooters at break time. Injury rates did not rise, and staff reported that pupils were more absorbed in their games.

D. Despite this evidence, children's freedom to play outdoors has shrunk dramatically. A recent national survey of 2,000 families asked grandparents and their grandchildren how far from home they had been allowed to go alone at the age of eight. The grandparents' average was 1.6 kilometres; for today's children it was just 280 metres. The same survey suggested that the time children spend playing outside each week has fallen by about half over the last thirty years.

E. The reasons for this decline are complex. Heavier traffic has made many streets genuinely less suitable for play, and parents frequently mention a fear of strangers, even though official figures show that such dangers have not increased. Homework and organised after-school activities fill more of the week than they once did. Screens are often blamed, but when the children in the survey were asked why they did not play outside more, the most common answer was that there was nobody else outside to play with. Outdoor play, it seems, depends on a critical mass of children: once most of them stay indoors, the rest tend to follow.

F. A number of communities are now trying to reverse the trend. In the town of Brindleford, two neighbours began closing their street to traffic for three hours one afternoon a month so that children could play safely on the road. The idea spread, and around sixty streets now take part, although some drivers complained at first about the closures. Other initiatives focus on schools. In 'loose parts' schemes, pupils are given old tyres, wooden crates and lengths of rope at lunchtime and left to decide what to make with them. Teachers taking part report fewer arguments between pupils, while some parents were initially concerned about muddy uniforms. Whether such schemes have any effect on academic results has not yet been studied.

G. None of this means that childhood should be returned to some imagined golden age, nor that organised activities have no value. The point, researchers argue, is balance. Children need some time and space in which adults are not directing every moment, and in which mild risks are treated as part of growing up rather than as failures of supervision. As Okafor-Lindqvist puts it, 'Often the most useful thing an adult can do is to step back and do nothing at all.'

script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the new Ashgrove Central Library. My name's Priya Lowell, and I'm the senior librarian here. I know many of you were regular users of the old building on Mill Street, so I'd like to spend about fifteen minutes explaining how things work here before you explore on your own.

First, a bit of background. The new building took just over three years to complete. Many people assume the main reason for the move was that the old library was too small, and it certainly was crowded. But the real problem was the roof, which had been leaking for years and was damaging the older parts of our collection.

The building itself was designed to use as little energy as possible. The large windows on the south side provide most of the light during the day, and the heating comes from pumps that draw warmth from the ground.
You may have read in the local paper about solar panels on the roof. In fact, they were dropped from the final plans because of the cost, although we hope to add them at a later stage.
Now, the layout. When you come in through the main entrance, you'll find the self-service machines immediately on your left. You can use these to borrow and return books, and also to pay any fines.

The information desk, where a member of staff is always available, is straight ahead of you, beside the lifts. If the machines aren't working, or you have a question about your account, that's the place to go.
Children's books and the café are on the ground floor. The first floor is home to adult fiction and non-fiction, along with our study area. Please note that the study area is for silent work only.

If you want to work with other people, for example on a college project, you'll need to book one of the meeting rooms on the second floor. You can do this online or at the information desk, and there's no charge.
The second floor also houses our new local history centre. This holds maps, photographs and newspapers going back over two hundred years.

Because many of these items are fragile, they can't be taken out of the room, and you'll need to make an appointment with our archivist if you want to see any of the original documents. Digital copies, however, can be viewed on the computers in the centre at any time.

One feature I'm particularly proud of is the rooftop terrace. It's open from April to October, and you're welcome to read up there or bring a packed lunch. Please remember, though, that your own food isn't allowed anywhere else in the building, including the study area and the history centre.
Finally, opening hours. During the week, we're open from nine until eight, and on Saturdays we close at five. On Sundays, which is new for us, we'll be open from eleven until three.
That Sunday opening is for a trial period of six months, and whether it continues will depend on how many people actually use it. So please do come along.
Right, I'll be at the information desk for the rest of the morning if you have any questions. Enjoy exploring your new library.

paragraphs: A. For much of the twentieth century, the public library had a clear and settled identity: a quiet building filled with books, where silence was enforced and borrowing was the main activity. In recent decades, however, that identity has come under pressure. The spread of the internet, the rise of e-books and repeated cuts to local government budgets have led many commentators to predict the slow decline of the library as an institution. Yet in a number of towns and cities, libraries are not disappearing but changing shape, often in ways their founders would scarcely recognise.

B. One of the most visible changes is the arrival of the makerspace. In the northern port town of Ellesmoor, the central library converted a little-used reference room into a workshop in 2019, equipping it with 3D printers, sewing machines and a laser cutter. According to the library's manager, Ruth Calloway, the room was intended mainly for teenagers, but the largest group of users turned out to be retired people, many of whom wanted to repair household items or learn skills they had never had time for during their working lives. Within two years, the makerspace was attracting more visitors per week than the adult fiction section.

C. A second development is the so-called 'library of things'. Rather than lending only books and films, some libraries now allow members to borrow tools, camping equipment, musical instruments and even kitchen appliances. The logic is straightforward: many households own items such as electric drills that are used for only a few minutes in their entire lifetime, and sharing them saves both money and resources. A survey carried out by the Branwell Institute, a research organisation that studies community services, found that members who borrowed tools were also more likely to borrow books, suggesting that new services can bring readers back rather than drawing them away.

D. Libraries are also positioning themselves as community hubs. Many now host job clubs, language cafés, health check-ups and advice sessions on housing or benefits. In some rural areas, the library is the last remaining public building in the village after the closure of the post office, the bank and the pub. For residents without a reliable internet connection at home, the library's free computers and wifi can be essential for tasks such as applying for work or contacting government departments, which are increasingly carried out only online.

E. These changes have not been universally welcomed. Some long-standing users complain that libraries have become noisy, and that the space given to workshops and events has been taken from book collections. In Ellesmoor, a petition signed by several hundred residents asked the council to restore a 'silent floor', which the library eventually agreed to do. Critics have also raised a more fundamental objection: if libraries try to be everything to everyone, they risk losing the specialist knowledge of trained librarians, whose skills in helping people find and judge information are arguably more valuable than ever in an age of misleading online content.

F. Funding presents another difficulty. Makerspaces and tool collections are expensive to set up, and equipment must be maintained, insured and eventually replaced. Many projects have relied on one-off grants from charities or local businesses, which leaves them vulnerable once the money runs out. Some libraries have experimented with charging small fees for the use of specialist machines, but this raises awkward questions for an institution traditionally founded on the principle of free access for all.

G. Despite these tensions, many observers argue that the library's core purpose has not really changed. In their view, the library has always existed to give people access to resources they could not easily afford on their own, whether those resources are books, a computer or a sewing machine. Seen in this light, the reinvention of the public library is less a break with its past than a continuation of it, and its future may depend on how skilfully it balances the new services with the quiet, book-filled spaces that many people still value.

script: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name's Rosalind Achebe, and I'm the organiser of the new Hollins Green Repair Café. I'd like to spend a few minutes telling you how it will work.

First of all, the idea. A repair café is not a shop. Nobody is paid, and we don't sell anything. Volunteers sit down with you and help you fix your own broken items, so that you learn how to do it yourself next time.

The idea for this one actually came from my neighbour. I'd assumed it would be the council that started something like this, or perhaps the local college, but it was Harold, a retired electrician, who knocked on my door with the suggestion last spring.

We'll meet once a month, on the last Saturday, from ten until one. We'd originally hoped to use the library, but it's closed at weekends, so instead we'll be in the hall at St Anne's Primary School, which has plenty of tables and good parking.

Now, what can you bring? Small electrical items such as lamps, kettles and radios are welcome, as are clothes, bicycles and toys. The one thing we can't accept is anything that runs on gas, like heaters or cookers. That's simply for safety reasons, and our insurance won't cover it.

People often ask what it costs. There's no fixed charge. We do put out a box for donations, and the money goes towards spare parts and tea. If a repair needs a new part, though, you'll have to buy that yourself, and we can tell you where to get it.

When you arrive, please go to the registration desk first. You'll fill in a short form describing the problem, and then you'll be given a number. That way, people are seen in the order they arrive, and our volunteers can be matched to the right job.

Speaking of volunteers, we already have twelve, which is a great start. What we're really short of, though, isn't electricians or tailors. We've got plenty of those. It's people who can repair furniture, especially chairs. So if you're good with wood, please come and talk to me.

We also need someone to help with publicity. At the moment, most people hear about us through the posters in the shop windows, but we'd like to set up a page on the community website, and that's where a volunteer would really help.

One last thing. At each session we'll be keeping a record of what comes in and whether it was fixed. Last year, at the trial session in the church, we repaired about two-thirds of the items. The aim is to show the council how much waste we're keeping out of landfill.
Our very first session is on the twenty-eighth of this month. Mugs of tea are free, and children are very welcome, as long as they're with an adult. So, does anyone have any questions?
Yes, the gentleman at the back... Ah, good question. Sharp tools stay with the volunteers, so you don't need to bring your own. Just bring the item, and any parts you've already bought. Thank you.

paragraphs: A. For most of human history, repairing things was simply part of ordinary life. A torn coat was patched, a cracked pot was bound with wire, and a broken chair was taken to a local craftsman rather than thrown away. In many towns, the cobbler, the tinker and the watchmender were as familiar as the baker. Repair was not regarded as a hobby or a moral choice; it was an economic necessity, because new goods were expensive and labour, by comparison, was cheap.

B. During the second half of the twentieth century, this balance shifted dramatically. Mass production lowered the price of manufactured goods, while wages rose steadily in industrialised countries. As a result, it frequently became cheaper to buy a replacement than to pay someone to fix the original. Historians of consumption, such as Liesel Varga in her study of post-war households, have argued that this period also saw a change in attitudes: owning new things became a sign of success, while mended items were associated with poverty.

C. Manufacturers responded to, and arguably encouraged, these changes. Products began to be designed in ways that made them difficult to open, with parts glued rather than screwed together. Spare parts were often available only to authorised dealers, and repair manuals were treated as commercial secrets. Critics describe the result as 'planned obsolescence', meaning the deliberate shortening of a product's useful life. Companies tend to reject this label, claiming that sealed designs are lighter, safer and more resistant to water and dust, and that customers themselves demand slim, attractive devices.

D. The environmental cost of this throwaway culture has become increasingly difficult to ignore. Electronic waste is now one of the fastest-growing categories of rubbish worldwide, and much of it contains valuable metals that are never recovered. When such waste is shipped abroad, it is often processed in unsafe conditions, exposing workers to toxic substances and polluting nearby soil and rivers. Even when devices are recycled properly, the energy used in manufacturing them is lost for good. A survey carried out by the Northfield Institute for Material Use found that the average household owned eleven devices that no longer worked but had not been thrown away, largely because their owners did not know how to dispose of them safely.

E. Since around 2010, however, there have been clear signs of a revival. Volunteer-run repair cafés have spread across Europe and beyond, offering free help in community halls and libraries. Online platforms now publish step-by-step guides written by amateurs, and video tutorials on replacing a phone battery can attract millions of viewers. Interestingly, the people who attend repair events are not mainly those on low incomes; organisers report that many visitors are well-educated professionals who are motivated less by saving money than by a desire to reduce waste.

F. At the same time, campaigners have pushed for what has become known as the 'right to repair'. This movement argues that consumers should be legally entitled to fix the products they own, or to choose an independent repairer, without losing their warranty. Several governments have introduced rules requiring manufacturers to supply spare parts for a minimum number of years after a product is sold. Some regions also oblige companies to publish a repairability score, so that shoppers can compare how easy different models are to fix before they buy.

G. Whether these measures will change behaviour in the long term remains uncertain. Supporters point out that the availability of parts alone does not guarantee that people will use them, particularly when repair skills have been lost over two or three generations. Others argue that the most important change must come at the design stage: a product built with standard screws and modular components is far more likely to be repaired than one that requires specialist tools. What does seem clear is that durability, once taken for granted and later almost forgotten, has returned as a serious public concern.

script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Inchmore Island. I'm Freya, and I'm the senior warden here. That means I live on the island from March until the end of September, together with two assistant wardens and, this year, four volunteers.

Before anything else, a word about the boat back. Normally it leaves from the jetty at four o'clock, but the forecast shows the wind picking up this afternoon, so the skipper has asked us to bring that forward to half past two.
Please don't be late. If the sea gets too rough, he can't come back for anyone, and we don't have beds for visitors.
You'll have noticed there's no café on Inchmore. There is fresh drinking water at the visitor hut, though, and the hut also has the only toilets on the island.
The island is about two kilometres long, and a path marked with white posts loops right round it. Please keep to the path at all times.

That isn't really for your safety. The ground is quite firm, and the cliff edges are fenced. It's because the grassy slope on the west side is full of puffin burrows, and they collapse very easily if someone steps on them.
Puffins are what most people come to see, of course, but do look out for our terns near the north beach. They're very protective of their nests and will dive at your head if you get too close.
If that happens, it simply means you've wandered too near. There's no need to wave your arms or run. Just walk calmly back the way you came, and they'll leave you alone.
We've had some good news this season. The puffin count in May came to just over two thousand one hundred birds, about three hundred more than last year.

Now, we'd love to take the credit, and our new nest monitoring has certainly helped us understand what's going on. But the main reason seems to be that sand eels, which the puffins feed to their chicks, have been far more plentiful in the waters round the island.

Some of you may have read that Inchmore once had a problem with rats. That's true, but they were removed in two thousand and nine, and the island has been rat-free ever since. That's why we check bags at the jetty: one rat hidden in a box of supplies could do enormous damage.

As for photography, you're very welcome to take pictures, and tripods are fine as long as they stay on the path. The best views are from the platform at Gull Rock rather than the north beach. Drones, however, aren't allowed anywhere on the island, as they frighten birds off their nests.

If you'd like to help the reserve, the easiest thing you can do today is fill in the sightings sheet at the visitor hut. We don't ask for donations, although there are membership leaflets in the hut, and volunteer applications for next season open in January.

Finally, last year we ran a guided walk to the north beach at one o'clock, but this year I'll be giving a short talk at the hut instead, about the grey seals that breed on the island's rocky eastern shore. Right, enjoy your morning.
listening.title: Part 2 · A warden's welcome talk

paragraphs: A. For centuries, remote islands have offered seabirds something the mainland cannot: safety. Species such as petrels, shearwaters and puffins spend most of their lives at sea, coming ashore only to breed, and many of them nest in burrows or on open ground where eggs and chicks are easily reached. On islands without land predators, this strategy works well. The difficulty is that very few islands have remained untouched. Rats, cats, stoats and mice, carried by ships either deliberately or by accident, are now thought to have reached around eighty per cent of the world's island groups, and their effect on ground-nesting birds can be devastating.

B. The story of Hollin Island, a 300-hectare outcrop in the North Atlantic, is typical. When naturalists first surveyed it in the 1890s, they described a colony of shearwaters so dense that the ground was 'hollow underfoot'. Brown rats are believed to have arrived in the 1930s, most likely from a supply boat that was wrecked on the eastern shore. By 2004, a survey team could find fewer than forty breeding pairs of shearwaters, and the island's storm petrels had disappeared altogether.

C. In recent decades, eradication rather than control has become the preferred response. Control, which involves trapping or poisoning a proportion of the animals each year, must be continued indefinitely, and a handful of survivors can rebuild a population within months. Eradication aims to remove every last individual in a single, intensive operation. On Hollin, the work was carried out in the winter of 2011, when the rats were short of natural food and therefore most likely to take bait, and when no seabirds were present to be harmed. Bait stations were laid out on a grid at fifty-metre intervals across the whole island, including sea cliffs that teams could reach only on ropes.

D. Yet the most demanding part of any project begins after the last rat has gone. An island can be declared predator-free only after two full years without any sign of the target species, and during that period, and indefinitely afterwards, it must be protected from reinvasion. On Hollin, every boat landing is now inspected, supplies arrive in sealed containers, and permanent detection devices, such as chew-cards and wax blocks that record tooth marks, are checked every month. Wardens point out that a single pregnant rat stepping ashore could undo a decade of effort.

E. Measuring success is not straightforward either. Burrow-nesting birds are hard to count because they are active on land mainly at night, and a burrow that looks occupied may in fact be empty. Researchers on Hollin therefore combine several methods. Small cameras lowered into a sample of burrows show whether an egg or chick is present, while sound recorders left out overnight provide a measure of overall activity. Volunteers have also begun playing recorded calls into burrows; a bird inside will often reply, a technique known as call playback.

F. The results so far have been encouraging, if slower than some supporters had hoped. Shearwater numbers on Hollin had risen to around 310 breeding pairs by 2023, and in 2020 storm petrels were heard calling on the island for the first time in half a century. Ecologists warn, however, that seabirds are long-lived and slow to breed: a shearwater may not raise its first chick until it is five or six years old. Recovery is therefore measured in decades rather than years, and some colonies may need encouragement, such as artificial nest boxes or loudspeakers that attract passing birds by broadcasting the calls of their own species.

G. Not everyone welcomes eradication. Poison can kill non-target species, and on inhabited islands the removal of cats in particular has sometimes caused bitter local disagreement. Supporters respond that, measured by the number of species protected for each pound spent, island restoration is among the most cost-effective forms of conservation available. With seabirds now one of the most threatened groups of birds in the world, many conservationists argue that the real question is no longer whether such projects should happen, but which islands should come first.
